They carry the evidence of Iran’s crackdown on their bodies. I stop people from bleeding to death. As a trauma and vascular interventional radiologist in Los Angeles, I find catastrophic bleeding and stop it within minutes. Still, I wasn’t prepared for what I saw in victims of Iran’s January protests inside and outside the country.

State TV host sparks backlash over ‘southern Iran for southern Lebanon’ remark. An Iranian state television presenter has sparked widespread criticism after saying “southern Iran be sacrificed for southern Lebanon” while dismissing criticism over the damage caused by recent US airstrikes on Iran’s southern provinces.

To survive maximum pressure, Iran kept pumping and broke its oil company. Donald Trump’s maximum pressure is usually scored by counting tankers and tracking the rial, but Iran’s budget points to a deeper cost: more than $80 billion in NIOC bank debt and sovereign-fund arrears, repeatedly deferred as Iranians shoulder the burden.

US rules out Iran truce extension as Tehran official sets new deadline. The 60-day period associated with the Iran-US interim peace deal ended Monday without a breakthrough, with Washington rejecting an extension and a senior Iranian official saying the US had a few weeks to meet the agreement’s terms before further talks.

Iran’s ‘infiltration’ bill sparks backlash over sweeping reach. A bill before Iran’s parliament that would impose new restrictions on contacts with foreign media, universities and organizations has drawn widespread objections over its potential impact on routine academic, cultural and civil-society activity.

Chinese state tankers avoid Strait of Hormuz, Bab al-Mandab – Reuters. Two Chinese state-controlled shipping companies have stopped sending oil tankers through the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab, instead loading crude outside the Persian Gulf amid heightened security risks, Reuters reported on Tuesday, citing industry sources and shipping data.

Forced to serve in the IRGC, now fighting to stay in Canada. Iranian men conscripted into the Revolutionary Guards for their compulsory military service fear they and their families could lose the right to remain in Canada, after letters warned the mandatory stint may amount to membership in a terrorist organization.

Leaked audio: Iran's Basij brace for new protests and fear being named online. Officials of Iran's Basij militia can be heard on a leaked recording weighing the risk of a new round of protests and the danger that members will be identified online, a rare glimpse of the anxiety inside the force the state sends against demonstrators.

Seven months on, January protests still shape Iranians’ lives. Seven months after the January massacre, Iranians answering an Iran International call-out describe lives still bent around it: sleep and nerves that never recovered, friendships remade or broken, politics hardened, and a future they struggle to picture.

Iran forces detain relatives of child killed in 2022 protests. Iranian security forces detained three relatives of the family of Kian Pirfalak, a nine-year-old killed during the 2022 protests, after raiding a village in the southern city of Izeh on Sunday evening, informed sources told Iran International.

Canada deports former Iranian official linked to 2019 protest crackdown. Canada has deported a former Iranian Interior Ministry spokesman who served during the deadly crackdown on nationwide protests in November 2019, Global News reported.

French source rejects Iran espionage allegations against diplomats. Allegations by Iran’s Intelligence Ministry that two French diplomats briefly detained in Tehran last month were involved in espionage are “completely false,” a French diplomatic source told Iran International.

For Iranian journalists, exile can last a lifetime. Journalists are not supposed to become the story. We are usually on the other side of it. Someone lives through an event and we write about it. Someone is gone and we report their passing. A crisis unfolds and we try to find the right words to tell its story.

Trump calls off Iran talks as Tehran doubles down on Hormuz leverage. President Donald Trump has halted diplomatic engagement with Iran until further notice, the White House said on Tuesday, as Tehran hardens its position over the Strait of Hormuz and presses Washington to meet its demands.

The 60-day deadline is over. Now what does Trump do with Iran?. With the 60-day period set by the June US-Iran memorandum now over and no final agreement in place, Washington faces a choice between intensifying pressure, renewing major strikes or settling into a prolonged and unstable holding pattern.

Iran weighs attacks on military targets in Europe – FT. Iran has considered attacking military targets in Europe if US President Donald Trump escalates the war, the Financial Times reported on Wednesday, citing two insiders.

Luxury Tehran property asking prices surpass Munich and Sydney. Some luxury apartments in northern Tehran are being advertised above the price of central Munich or Sydney: 25 billion rials, about $13,228, per square meter, according to Farhikhtegan newspaper, which examined the listings.

An Iranian film broke every taboo. Viewers say society broke them first. An Iranian film made in defiance of the censors reached YouTube last week, and the argument it started was not the one its makers might have expected: many viewers are asking not whether Bidad goes too far, but whether it goes far enough for the country it depicts.

Ex-president warns Iran against losing ‘unprecedented’ opportunity with Trump. Former Iranian President Mohammad Khatami has strongly backed the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding signed by US President Donald Trump and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, warning that Iran could face serious problems if the opportunity created by it is lost.

Pezeshkian admin says infiltration bill violates rights, could drive brain drain. President Masoud Pezeshkian's government has formally opposed a bill aimed at countering foreign intelligence infiltration, saying it violates citizens' rights, restricts academic ties and could accelerate the emigration of Iranian experts and researchers.

Tehran gas stations run dry as fuel price hike fears mount. Gas stations in parts of Tehran closed after running out of fuel Wednesday, while motorists elsewhere in the Iranian capital waited up to an hour to fill their tanks amid mounting fears of a fuel price hike, locals told Iran International.
The unlikely return of European diplomacy in the Iran-US conflict. For years, diplomacy between Iran and the United States has largely been conducted through a familiar group of intermediaries.

« Ras Bath est un danger pour la transition » : ce qu’il faut retenir de la condamnation de l’activiste malien. Ras Bath et Rose la vie chère, incarcérés depuis mars 2023, ont été reconnus coupables d’atteinte à la sûreté de l’État par la justice malienne. Les deux activistes ont été condamnés à 10 ans de prison, dont trois avec sursis.

Rabiu contre Dangote : deux milliardaires à la lutte pour bâtir l’avenir industriel du Nigeria. Abdul Samad Rabiu et Aliko Dangote sont les hommes les plus riches du Nigeria. Ils s’affrontent à coups de milliards de dollars d’investissement dans le ciment, le sucre, les engrais… Chacun, à sa manière, veut transformer le paysage industriel du pays.
Comment la dette africaine séduit les investisseurs. La dette locale africaine retrouve les faveurs des marchés. Mais les pays de la zone CFA restent en marge de cet élan.

Gabon : Aurélien Mintsa Nguema, le discret mais influent frère, trésorier et diplomate du président. Le frère cadet de Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema a longtemps tenté de se tenir à l’écart des médias et des querelles de cour. De passage à Paris, le nouvel ambassadeur du Gabon en Inde a toutefois accepté de se confier à Jeune Afrique.

Aminata Kane (Visa) : « La régulation des fintech est un peu plus contraignante en Afrique francophone ». Si l’Afrique subsaharienne figure parmi les marchés où les transactions mobiles progressent le plus rapidement, plusieurs freins entravent encore leur développement à plus grande échelle, estime la vice-présidente senior de Visa pour l’Afrique de l’Ouest et l’Afrique centrale.

Cameroun : le resort de Ngomedzap, fief politique de Grégoire Owona. Le ministre camerounais du Travail, Grégoire Owona, a fait construire dans son village natal un resort assorti d’un parcours de golf. Une destination de loisirs, mais pas uniquement…

Tchad : Mahamat Idriss Déby Itno est-il vraiment un souverainiste ?. Retrait des troupes françaises, rapprochement avec l’AES, départ annoncé de la CPI : le président tchadien assume un discours de plus en plus « populiste ». Mais derrière cette rupture affichée, les réalités sont plus nuancées.

Le port de Tema fourbit ses armes face à Abidjan et Lomé. Alors que la compétition est rude entre les ports d’Afrique de l’Ouest, l’infrastructure ghanéenne de Tema consolide son essor. Une réussite fondée sur la croissance du trafic de conteneurs que le port veut appliquer aux autres segments d’activité.

Au Sénégal, l’Assemblée nationale adopte la loi sur la déclaration de patrimoine des hauts dirigeants. Le nouveau texte impose au chef de l’État, au président de l’Assemblée nationale et au Premier ministre de déclarer leur patrimoine au Conseil constitutionnel à leur entrée et à leur sortie de fonction. Un texte adopté sur fond de discorde entre Bassirou Diomaye Faye et Ousmane Sonko.

Zambie : Hakainde Hichilema réélu président avec 60 % des voix malgré des tensions inédites. Le président sortant a été réélu pour un deuxième mandat à la tête de la Zambie dans une confusion politique inhabituelle. Plusieurs opposants ont été arrêtés.

Cameroun : 5 questions pour comprendre le scandale des faux décrets de Paul Biya. Le 12 juin, deux faux décrets présidentiels ont failli être lus à la CRTV. Deux mois plus tard, l’enquête s’oriente vers l’entourage de Paul Biya et met en lumière l’exacerbation de la lutte entre les clans qui se disputent le poste, encore vacant, de vice-président.

Nigeria : la fin de l’eldorado des cryptos ?. Le Nigeria veut taxer les cryptomonnaies. Les opérateurs du secteur redoutent une fuite des capitaux vers des plateformes étrangères non réglementées, au détriment du premier marché d’actifs numériques du continent.

En Centrafrique, François Bozizé mis en cause dans la disparition de Charles Massi lors du procès « Bossembélé ». L’ex-compagne de Charles Massi a livré un témoignage accablant devant la Cour pénale spéciale contre François Bozizé, jugé par contumace pour des crimes de guerre commis au camp militaire de Bossembélé.

En Côte d’Ivoire, comment les anciens chefs rebelles ont conquis le sommet de l’État. Vingt-quatre ans après l’insurrection de 2002, les anciens chefs des Forces nouvelles dirigent états-majors, préfectures et ambassades. Le décès de Martin Fofié Kouakou rappelle comment cette génération de « comzone » a reconfiguré les institutions.

Maroc : derrière les records de croissance, les failles d’un modèle social. Les capitaux affluent et les grands chantiers s’enchaînent, mais l’emploi est à la traîne, la population vieillit et les inégalités demeurent. Le rapport annuel du Conseil économique, social et environnemental (Cese) montre que le passage de la croissance au progrès social reste difficile.

Dialogue en RDC : face à Félix Tshisekedi, le dilemme de l’opposition. La coalition C64 a promis une nouvelle manifestation devant le Parlement congolais, le 15 septembre. Mais ces deux derniers mois, les opposants ont souvent été contraints de s’adapter au timing imposé par Félix Tshisekedi.

Côte d’Ivoire : la concurrence s’accentue dans le monde des moulins. Déjà très compétitif, le secteur ivoirien de la minoterie voit arriver un nouvel acteur. Un dynamisme porté par la croissance et l’essor démographique de ces dernières années.

Cameroun : Grégoire Mba Mba, prince de Kribi et de l’Océan ad vitam aeternam ?. Responsables politiques et hommes d’affaires se ruent sur les terres qui entourent la ville de Kribi. Mais le sénateur Mba Mba entend bien rester le patron de cette partie de la côte méridionale du Cameroun.

Diomaye, l’affranchi : pourquoi le président sénégalais joue sa survie politique après la rupture avec Sonko. Après avoir limogé Ousmane Sonko, son Premier ministre, Bassirou Diomaye Faye, le chef de l’État sénégalais, qui vient de créer son propre parti, a les yeux rivés sur les échéances électorales qui, en 2027, détermineront son destin politique.

L’affaire Bruno Foucher, dernier épisode d’une série de crises pour l’ambassade française en Centrafrique. Le scandale provoqué par l’ambassadeur de France, qui a reconnu avoir reçu de nombreuses jeunes femmes dans sa résidence, est le dernier d’une longue succession d’affaires. Il intervient en outre au pire moment pour Paris, qui tente de reprendre pied en Centrafrique malgré l’omniprésence russe dans le pays.

RDC : avec Starlink Mobile, Airtel est-il en passe de bousculer le marché ?. La RDC devient le premier pays africain à bénéficier de Starlink Mobile, via Airtel. Un accord potentiellement étendu aux 14 filiales du groupe sur le continent, mais dont l’impact reste conditionné à la disponibilité de terminaux haut de gamme.

Archives coloniales du Maroc : entre fonds stratégiques et piège d’une réduction du récit national. Du fait de la colonisation, une grande partie des archives marocaines est encore conservée à l’étranger, notamment en France et en Espagne. Alors que le royaume mène une politique active de récupération de ces documents et que Paris comme Madrid se disent prêts à les lui transmettre, les historiens rappellent que l’étude du passé ne se limite pas à la période du protectorat.

Côte d’Ivoire : Adama Bictogo à « Yop City », loin du perchoir mais pas du pouvoir. Quelques mois après avoir quitté la présidence de l’Assemblée nationale, Adama Bictogo investit désormais son énergie à Yopougon, à la tête de la Snedai, le groupe qu’il a fondé, mais aussi auprès de sa famille. Portrait d’un homme qui patiente, sans rien céder de sa loyauté envers Alassane Ouattara.

Tony Elumelu, le tycoon qui rêve de faire de Seplat Energy un UBA du pétrole. Élu président de Seplat Energy en juin 2025, Tony Elumelu ambitionne de bâtir un champion pétrolier nigérian à l’image de ce qu’il a réalisé avec UBA dans la banque. Un pari autrement plus contraint.

Togo : ce que l’on sait de l’arrestation des deux journalistes français placés en détention à Lomé. Deux journalistes français ainsi que leur collaborateur togolais, interpellés fin juillet dans le nord du pays, ont été placés en détention lundi 17 août. Ils sont poursuivis pour « fausses déclarations ». Selon nos informations, ils bénéficiaient pourtant d’une autorisation de tournage.

FMI au Sénégal : trois enjeux clés pour sortir de l’impasse de la dette cachée. Alors qu’une nouvelle mission du FMI débute ce 19 août au Sénégal, le pays n’a jamais été aussi proche d’un accord avec le Fonds. Les discussions pourraient néanmoins se prolonger pendant encore plusieurs semaines. Explications.

Guinée : Abdourahmane Bella Bah condamné à un mois de prison ferme. L’activiste, connu pour ses prises de position critiques sur les réseaux sociaux, était accusé d’avoir tenu des propos injurieux et diffamatoires à l’encontre du premier imam de la Grande Mosquée de Conakry.

RDC : Joseph Kabila riposte à Washington après les sanctions du Trésor américain. Ciblé en avril par le Trésor américain, qui l’accuse de soutenir les rebelles de l’AFC/M23, l’ex-président congolais organise sa défense aux États-Unis. Il a notamment sollicité un avocat sur place pour contester les sanctions qui le visent.

Fonds souverain guinéen : les dessous du bras de fer entre Conakry et le FMI. Conakry envisage de créer un fonds souverain doté de 1 milliard de dollars pour abriter les revenus de Simandou. Le FMI et la Banque mondiale émettent des réserves. Coulisses.

Cameroun : Nkolandom, chefferie et baronnie du ministre Jacques Fame Ndongo. Propriété du ministre de l’Enseignement supérieur, le Centre touristique de Nkolandom, refuge naturel et espace de préservation de la mémoire patrimoniale, situé dans le sud du pays, est surtout un lieu de rencontres discrètes entre caciques du parti présidentiel.

Coupe d’Afrique des nations féminine : le Malawi à une victoire de l’un des plus beaux exploits du tournoi. Les Scorchers, emmenées par les sœurs Temwa et Tabitha Chawinga, ont déjoué tous les pronostics en se qualifiant pour la finale, qu’elles disputent contre le Cameroun, dimanche à Rabat. L’équipe, 153ᵉ au classement mondial, n’avait jusqu’alors jamais pris part à la compétition.

« The Polygamist » sur Netflix, la série sud-africaine à succès qui torpille le patriarcat. L’histoire des vies parallèles d’un magnat de l’immobilier narcissique est devenue l’une des dix séries non anglophones les plus regardées sur la plateforme américaine.

Ebola en RDC : l’épidémie devient la plus meurtrière de l’histoire du pays en seulement trois mois. Sur les 4 945 cas de contaminations confirmées, 2 325 personnes sont mortes, selon le dernier bilan des autorités congolaises.

Au Mali, la condamnation des activistes « Ras Bath » et « Rose Vie chère », symbole de la répression croissante des voix critiques à l’égard de la junte du général Assimi Goïta. La cour d’appel de Bamako a condamné, lundi, les deux militants à dix ans de prison. Cette décision, dénoncée par leur défense comme politiquement motivée, illustre le durcissement de la répression contre les voix dissidentes.

Naufrage en Méditerranée : 7 migrants sont morts et 50 autres ont été secourus au large de la Libye. Quarante-cinq hommes et cinq femmes secourus, dont vingt-neuf mineurs non accompagnés, étaient à bord d’une petite embarcation en bois. Ils affirment être originaires d’Egypte et de Somalie, selon l’ONG Emergency.

Zimbabwe : le bilan du naufrage d’un ferry sur le lac Kariba s’alourdit encore, passant à 92 morts. Des centaines de personnes ont défilé au cours du week-end à l’hôpital de district de Kariba, faisant la queue pour identifier les corps de leurs proches.

En Libye, l’autorité du maréchal Haftar écornée par la rivalité entre ses fils. Khalifa Haftar, 82 ans, a bâti son image d’homme fort de la Cyrénaïque en réprimant toute contestation. La stabilité dans l’Est libyen est aujourd’hui menacée, alors que le maréchal prépare sa succession et que le patron du renseignement militaire vient d’être assassiné.

VIDEO CAN : les Lionnes indomptables accueillies en héroïnes au Cameroun. Après sa victoire 3 buts à 0 face au Malawi, l’équipe camerounaise est revenue à Yaoundé avec son premier titre dans la compétition.

Au Nigeria, au moins 24 morts dans des attaques communautaires dans l’Etat du Plateau. Située au centre du pays, la région est le théâtre de violences récurrentes entre éleveurs musulmans itinérants et agriculteurs sédentaires chrétiens.

L’épidémie d’Ebola en RDC est « loin d’être maîtrisée » et il existe un « risque élevé d’une propagation internationale ». Actuellement, l’OMS juge le niveau de risque pour la santé publique « très élevé » pour la RDC, « élevé » pour l’Ouganda et les autres pays frontaliers de la RDC, et « faible » pour le reste de l’Afrique et du monde.

Patrick Vieira à la tête de l’équipe du Sénégal, pour sa première expérience de sélectionneur. La Fédération sénégalaise de football a officialisé, mardi, l’arrivée du champion du monde 1998 sur le banc des Lions de la Teranga. La Coupe du monde décevante de la sélection africaine avait contribué au licenciement de son prédécesseur, Pape Thiaw.

« Si j’ai mis ma fille dans une bouée et que je l’ai poussée dans l’eau, c’est pour son avenir » : l’horizon bouché de cette jeunesse du Maroc qui veut rejoindre Ceuta. La jeunesse marocaine, de plus en plus diplômée et connectée, se heurte à la précarité, aux salaires faibles et à un coût de la vie qui interdit l’autonomie. Les jeunes rencontrés par « Le Monde » dans le nord du royaume racontent une même impasse, qui les a poussés à tenter, fin juillet, de gagner l’enclave espagnole à la nage.

Deux Français arrêtés et détenus au Togo depuis le 27 juillet, selon le Quai d’Orsay. Il s’agit de deux réalisateurs travaillant pour une société de production française, selon le ministère des affaires étrangères français, dont la production devait être diffusée sur France Télévisions, d’après des médias locaux.

En Zambie, le président sortant, Hakainde Hichilema, réélu, son principal adversaire conteste le résultat. Dénonçant des restrictions et des actes d’intimidation pendant la campagne, son principal concurrent, Brian Mundubile, a déclaré qu’il « présenterait des preuves aux instances judiciaires compétentes et qu’il épuiserait toutes les voies légales ».

A Madagascar, « entre désir de liberté et attachement aux traditions », la « gen Z » photographiée par Charlotte Yonga. « Jeunesse en milieux hostiles » (6/7). A Madagascar, la « gen Z » a été à l’origine d’un vaste mouvement de contestation qui, en 2025, a fait tomber le pouvoir en place. Un an plus tôt, la photographe franco-camerounaise Charlotte Yonga avait fait poser ces jeunes, sans perspectives d’avenir, dans leur intimité. Des portraits qu’elle met en dialogue avec des paysages luxuriants. Un travail exposé cet été dans le cadre des Rencontres de la photographie d’Arles.

Angélique Kidjo devient la première chanteuse africaine à avoir son étoile sur le Walk of Fame d’Hollywood. Cette récompense arrive après plus de quarante ans de carrière et 18 albums pour l’artiste franco-béninoise, qui a inauguré son étoile ce mardi à Los Angeles.

Les Etats-Unis vont expulser jusqu’à 1 200 personnes au Liberia d’ici un an. Donald Trump a élargi le nombre de personnes susceptibles d’être expulsées, ciblant notamment celles qui bénéficiaient de protections juridiques leur permettant, sous les administrations précédentes, de vivre et de travailler aux Etats-Unis en raison de risques de persécutions dans leurs pays d’origine.

Au Kenya, le recours croissant aux « goons », ces gros bras payés pour semer le chaos dans les meetings politiques. Embauchés par des reponsables politiques pour assurer leur sécurité ou intimider leurs rivaux, ces jeunes n’hésitent pas à faire preuve de violence. Dimanche, un rassemblement du mouvement d’opposition Linda Mwananchi a été attaqué dans l’ouest du pays. A un an de l’élection présidentielle, le phénomène inquiète.

En Centrafrique, un éboulement dans une mine d’or artisanale fait au moins 100 morts. L’effondrement a eu lieu mardi à la mi-journée dans l’ouest du pays, à la frontière avec le Cameroun. Les opérations de secours se poursuivent.

L’arrestation de deux journalistes français au Togo, reflet de la dégradation des relations entre Paris et Lomé. Arrêtés fin juillet alors qu’ils tournaient les dernières images d’un documentaire dans le nord du pays, deux réalisateurs français sont détenus à Lomé et poursuivis pour de supposées fausses déclarations liées à leur visa.

Greece's alliance with Israel is becoming a domestic liability Submitted by Iason Athanasiadis on Wed, 08/19/2026 - 13:45 Athens sees Israel as an important partner, but the relationship is facing mounting anger over arms sales, high rents and Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza Israel issued a rare warning to its citizens in Greece last Sunday ahead of nationwide pro- Palestine protests: avoid advertising your nationality in public. The warning was striking in a country that Israelis have long regarded as a close ally, tourist and investment destination, and even a potential relocation haven. But Israel's relationship with Greece is becoming increasingly complicated. Rising rents, which many Greeks blame on Israeli property purchases, anger over Israelis jeering at pro-Palestinian demonstrations and Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis' close friendship with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu are all fuelling anger. "It's an asymmetrical relationship, where one side is powerful and the other powerless," Konstantinos Isychos, a former deputy defence minister who is opposed to the alliance, told Middle East Eye. "Developing relations with Israel is a double suicide because, were the genocide to pass unnoticed and unpunished, it sets a criminal precedent and could be repeated again." The hostility is reflected in public opinion. A 2026 Pew Research poll found that 65 percent of Greeks opposed the partnership, although many view it as a necessary evil because of what they perceive as an expansionist Turkey. On the streets, meanwhile, pro-Palestinian protests are vastly larger than the smattering of pro-Israeli ones. For some Greeks, opposition to the relationship is increasingly inseparable from the money Athens is spending on Israeli weapons and surveillance technology during Israel's genocidal war on Gaza . "There's never money available for better hospitals, firefighting aeroplanes, trains or pensions," Iason Apostolopoulos, a pro-Palestine activist and rescuer of migrants in the Central Mediterranean for Italian association Mediterranea Saving Humans, told MEE. "But there's always funds for purchasing Predator [a surveillance programme] and arms packages from Israel that feed a military machine that daily produces occupation, death and apartheid." That growing backlash is now being felt by Israelis who once saw Greece as an attractive escape from a country they regard as increasingly expensive, violent and dysfunctional. Nearly 100,000 Israelis left their country for more than three months in 2025, marking a third record year. Emigrants, who tend to be critical of Netanyahu’s policies, cite the constant threat of missile barrages and high cost of living as primary reasons for leaving. "Buying property in Greece and Cyprus became the secular response to the settler project," Ehud Eiran, an associate professor of political science at the University of Haifa, told MEE. "Whereas the project of the Orthodox was to go to the mountains and be religious, the project of the secular is to go West and buy property there." Building up a partnership According to Eiran, early Zionists originally sought to be accepted within the region in the hope that Israel could be negotiated out of the Ottoman empire. David Ben Gurion studied in Istanbul, while early diplomat Abba Eban studied Arabic at Cambridge. "Jewish pirates would join Muslims in attacking Christian galleys," Eiran noted, "and the few Jews involved in the naval battle of Lepanto, where the Ottomans clashed with Christendom, fought under the Ottoman flag." In Greece, Israelis find cheap property, nightlife and political refuge Read More » But the early idea that Israel as a state could find a place within the region was severely undermined by the events surrounding Israel’s creation and the conflicts that followed. Although current Israeli allies like Greece and India joined Muslim-majority countries like Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Iran and Turkey to vote against the UN Partition Plan for Palestine in 1947, it passed. Fighting immediately broke out between Palestine's Jewish and Arab communities, prompting the British mandate authorities to withdraw instead of seeking to implement it. Israel won four wars in a row in 1948, 1956, 1967 and 1973, prompting neighbours like Egypt and Jordan to begin concluding peace with it. These deals lacked popularity but offered strategic depth. The Abraham Accords initiated a fresh series of agreements in 2020, the most enthusiastic of which have been with Morocco and the UAE. The subsequent rejection of Israel by much of the region eventually pushed the country towards alternative forms of regional integration, including a partnership with Greece. The relationship has since developed from discreet military cooperation into one of Israel's most important strategic partnerships in the Mediterranean. Greece and Cyprus offer Israel diplomatic and industrial access into the European Union, while permitting Israeli forces to simulate bombing or fighting in terrain similar to its regional antagonists. Cyprus offers Israel access to a Lebanon-facing naval base, while the half of the island under Turkish military occupation is of interest since it brings Ankara into closer missile range. The three countries are connecting their electricity grids, developing submarine natural gas reserves and discussing joint patrols in the Eastern Mediterranean. A turning point came in 2010, when former Greek Prime Minister Yorgos Papandreou bumped into Netanyahu in a Moscow restaurant and invited him for dinner. The meeting helped pave the way for a closer relationship between the two countries. Yet cooperation had existed long before then. Although Greece was among the last western countries to recognise Israel, in 1990, the Greek military junta secretly purchased weapons from Israel in the 1960s and discussed establishing joint arms factories. That relationship was interrupted by the restoration of democracy in 1975, but ties resumed in the 1990s through intelligence and military cooperation. They became public in 2002 and expanded as relations between Israel and Turkey deteriorated. Israeli fighter jets began using Greek airspace for training, giving Israel an important opportunity to prepare for long-range operations. 'The relationship with Israel puts Greece in a position to regulate situations in the Mediterranean and the Middle East' - Alexandros Itimoudis, geopolitical analyst "The average Israeli doesn't know that the ease with which their airforce flew to Tehran, including midair refuellings, was due to the training they had the opportunity to do over Greece," Angelos Raphael, a translator and tour guide living in Israel, told MEE. In 2015, Greece became only the second country after the US to sign a military cooperation agreement with Israel, allowing the two countries to host each other's troops and materiel. "A lot more must have been agreed on than was announced," said Isychos, whose tenure as deputy defence minister coincided with the signing but who was at daggers drawn with his minister. The discovery of gas in the Eastern Mediterranean provided another incentive for closer cooperation. "When we discovered gas fields in around 2010, we suddenly went from being an energy-poor country to an energy exporter," said Eiran. "We settled maritime borders with Cyprus, planned to lay pipes and an electric connector from here to Greece... it was easier for us to talk publicly about energy and infrastructure rather than about Turkey as a common foe." What began as an energy and security partnership has since developed into a much broader strategic relationship, centred on military cooperation, intelligence and the positioning of Israel and its allies around the Mediterranean. Consequences of the Mecca Pact That role has become even more important as Israel faces a changing regional security environment. When Turkey signed a mutual defence pact on 7 August with economic heavyweight Saudi Arabia and nuclear-armed Pakistan, officials were careful to say the new alliance was not directed against any particular country, especially Iran. But the absence of Egypt and the strategic weight of the three countries led to growing speculation in Israel that it was, in practice, directed at Israel. "It could have extremely serious consequences both in the Mediterranean and on the Syrian front," Israeli Diaspora Affairs Minister Amichai Chikli warned, "and it requires us to deepen our alliances with Greece, Cyprus, the UAE, Somaliland and India." For years, Israel has been assembling what Netanyahu described as a "hexagon of alliances". The partnerships are heavily maritime-focused, extending from the Indian Ocean through India, across the Persian Gulf via the UAE, into the Red Sea through Somaliland, and across the Mediterranean through Greece, Cyprus and Morocco. Why the Mecca Agreement has given the UAE-Israel alliance the jitters Read More » Remarkably, Israel's choices of allies are all situated in or near strategic maritime chokepoints: Morocco is on one side of Gibraltar, controlling access to the Mediterranean; Greece controls the approach to the Turkish Straits; Somaliland sits opposite the Bab el-Mandeb bottleneck accessing the Red Sea; and the UAE bestrides both sides of Hormuz. Greece and Cyprus, meanwhile, give Israel strategic depth in the Eastern Mediterranean. "The relationship with Israel puts Greece in a position to regulate situations in the Mediterranean and the Middle East," Alexandros Itimoudis, a geopolitical analyst, told MEE. "We give Israel strategic depth, knowing that they have a supportive Greece and Cyprus in the sea behind them." With the Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb currently out of bounds to Israel because of military action by Iran and Yemen's Houthis, the Mediterranean has assumed greater importance. Israel has deepened intelligence and defence cooperation with Morocco, alongside diplomatic support for Rabat’s claim over the Spanish semi-enclave of Ceuta. In the Eastern Mediterranean, meanwhile, it has strengthened ties with Greece and Cyprus, while supplying weapons that form part of a broader security network facing their common Turkish adversary. But Israeli analysts are careful not to overstate the relationship. "It's a strong partnership but I wouldn't call it an alliance," said Gallia Lindenstrauss, a specialist on the Eastern Mediterranean at Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies. "There's a building up of independent capabilities but without expectations that the sides will come to each other as help in dealing with the adversary in times of conflict." Arms sales and positioning The strategic relationship is perhaps most visible in the rapid expansion of Israeli arms sales to Greece. Israel completed a hat-trick of major Mediterranean air-defence sales in July when Greece agreed to a €3bn deal involving many of the same systems sold to Morocco and Cyprus in 2022. The agreement will give Greece a unified national air-defence system while potentially linking Israeli-dominated air-awareness networks at opposite ends of the Mediterranean - possibly through hidden protocols sharing telemetry and offering a backdoor switch into the equipment's source code. There have also been questions over whether the anti-missile shield Greece provided to Saudi Arabia could contain a Trojan Horse element benefiting Tel Aviv. Has Greece become Israel's Trojan Horse in the Gulf? Read More » In April, Greece agreed to spend €650m on 36 rocket artillery launchers, precision-guided missiles with ranges of up to 300km, loitering munitions and a 10-year support package from Israel’s largest arms manufacturer, Elbit Systems. In August, Athens bought €1.5m worth of armoured vehicles from Israeli manufacturer Shladot, building on an earlier deal with the Greek police to acquire the rugged vehicles frequently seen in media coverage of the occupied West Bank. Greece also plans to co-produce a hard-to-detect submarine spy drone, the Blue Whale, with Israel Aerospace Industries. The vessel can remain submerged for up to a month. For critics of the partnership, the appeal of Israeli military technology is inseparable from its use in Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza and decades of occupation. "Israel's arms industry owes its success to its ability to test its weapons on Palestinians, proving through these endless human labs how useful they are," Yaar Dagan, a lecturer in international law at Middlesex University and author of the forthcoming title Drones, Settler Colonialism, and the Law: How Israel Became a Drone Superpower , told MEE. "What other country can prove that they've tested their weapons on thousands of people in thousands of locales?" The €3bn air-defence system will also be interoperable with Nato's Link 16 cryptographic communications system, further integrating Greece into a wider military architecture. AI development The relationship is moving beyond conventional arms sales into artificial intelligence and military data systems. Greece is developing an artificial intelligence-powered Command and Control (C2) network designed to combine data from existing Greek sensors and radars with Nato-standard information from Greek F-16s and F-35s and feed it into the Achilles Shield system. A custom-built Israeli C4I control centre will combine inputs from Israeli-purchased ELM-2084 radars and Greek fighter jets, allowing the system to track enemy drones in real time and minimise data-transfer delays. "No system offers 100 percent protection and we still don’t know how it will react in real-world conditions," retired Lieutenant-General Konstantinos Loukopoulos told MEE. 'Greece has great brains but because it's largely corrupt, it fails to maximise them' - Benny Nathan, professor at Technion "After all, look how many times the Iron Dome or even the Patriot, which is a standalone system, have been penetrated by Iranian missiles." The Achilles Shield forms part of the biggest defence overhaul in modern Greek history. Defence spending has risen from $5.5bn in 2019 to more than $8bn a year. Under its 2030 project, Greece plans to spend nearly €28bn on military modernisation by 2036, taking defence spending to 3.5 percent of GDP. Its purchases include three C-390 Millennium transport and refuelling aircraft, Hellfire missiles for Apache helicopters and sonar systems for frigates. "Greece is not preparing only for a traditional conflict involving aircraft, ships and armoured units," Aleksander Olech wrote in Defence 24. "It is preparing for a high-intensity battlefield in which drones, missiles, electronic warfare and the speed of data processing will determine the effectiveness of the armed forces." But Athens is seeking more than access to Israeli weapons. It wants to develop and manufacture military technology jointly, using cooperation with Israel to gain expertise and technology while making greater use of its own pool of engineers and scientists. Israel, however, sees an opportunity of its own. "Greece has great brains but because it's largely corrupt, it fails to maximise them," said Benny Nathan, a Greek-Israeli professor at the Faculty of Aerospace Engineering at Technion, Israel's primary technological university. "It wants to exploit them so they can function more like Israel's talents function, meaning that Israel wins the brains and Greece gets the know-how." Israel’s use of AI in Gaza is a terrifying model coming to a country near you Read More » Israeli companies have also expanded their footprint in Greece’s defence sector, acquiring companies that can apply for European Union defence-sector funding. Turkey has pursued a similar strategy by acquiring defence companies in Italy. The partnership has extended into surveillance technology, too. Israel has authorised the sale of sophisticated spyware such as Predator and Pegasus to Greece and Morocco, respectively, and possibly to Cyprus. The software is believed to contain a technological backdoor, potentially allowing Israel to benefit diplomatically from access to intercepted communications. For Greece, however, the growing strategic value of the partnership comes with a political cost. The closer the two countries become militarily, the harder it is for Athens to separate its relationship with Israel from the public anger generated by Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza. Ordinary Greeks and Cypriots increasingly criticise their country’s partnership with Israel, fearing a form of soft colonisation, and point to proposals to purchase Greek islands or examples where Israeli investors blocked off access to the coast or to entire villages following their purchases. And as Israel seeks to build a network of Mediterranean alliances to compensate for a rapidly changing regional environment, Greece is finding itself at the centre of a relationship that many of its citizens increasingly question. Foreign interference is real - but the UK should look beyond the usual culprits Submitted by Mustafa al-Dabbagh on Thu, 08/13/2026 - 13:16 Foreign money and foreign direction should be treated as a problem regardless of which state masterminds it An Extinction Rebellion protest outside 55 Tufton Street on 20 December 2025. Tufton Street houses think tanks and lobby groups that have shaped UK policy (Andrea Domeniconi/SOPA Images via Reuters Connect) On Last month the British government added interference in the democratic process to the National Risk Register , ranking it alongside cyberattack and pandemic as a threat to national security. The framing is consistent, and mostly justified: the National Security Act 2023 , the Foreign Influence Registration Scheme, and the Defending Democracy Taskforce target China, Russia, Iran and North Korea, and parliament's committees have documented sustained hostile efforts to shape British politics. But the scrutiny rarely extends past those names, even though other states have made attempts of their own. Peers raised this in a House of Lords debate that prompted ministers to order a review, with Lord Wallace of Saltaire telling the House the money came "from the United States and the UAE , as well as from hostile states such as Russia and China". Philip Rycroft's own March 2026 review went further, warning of "an emerging willingness of foreign actors and private citizens, including from allies like the United States, to interfere in, and influence, politics abroad". The government accepted that finding in July but hasn't acted like it. Months later, when an Israel-based advocacy body appeared at the same House of Lords accusing British Muslims of importing foreign influence, nobody asked it the question already asked of everyone else. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); NGO Monitor was founded inside the Jerusalem Center for Public Affairs , a right-leaning Israeli think tank whose president at the time, Isidore "Dore" Gold , was simultaneously a serving adviser to two Israeli prime ministers. Its founder, Gerald Steinberg, has been a paid consultant to the Israeli foreign ministry and National Security Council . Its funding runs through an opaque American vehicle backed by committed pro-Israel donors. Israeli lobbying and US opacity The Dutch foreign ministry found NGO Monitor's work rests on "selective citations, half-facts and insinuations" . A UN special rapporteur said in September 2024 that NGO Monitor ran a "vitriolic online smear campaign" against a Palestinian human rights group. It has company in the UK in the form of UK Lawyers for Israel (UKLFI). An Israeli government document showed UKLFI’s chief executive, Jonathan Turner , and his wife meeting a senior Israeli justice ministry official in 2019, seeking help against a British charity and a Palestinian children's NGO. The group's methods have been described as lawfare , legal threats meant to intimidate rather than win in court. A single letter got Chelsea and Westminster Hospital to remove a display of plates painted by children in Gaza. From 'absolute monarchy' to dear friend: How Nigel Farage and Reform learned to love the UAE Read More » Turner has admitted his group's "support" for Israel's Ministry of Strategic Affairs, which runs defamation campaigns against rights groups abroad, and UKLFI has settled a libel claim after falsely accusing a charity of funding terrorism. It now sits under Charity Commission investigation over hidden funding, with the outcome still not clear. None of this, it seems, counts as the interference it plainly is. The same week at NGO Monitor's House of Lords event, the Guardian revealed that the US State Department plans to hand $12m, awarded directly with no competition, to right-wing organisations founded by Jacob Rees-Mogg and Toby Young, framed as support for shared "civilizational bonds". Earlier this year, Young's own Free Speech Union got a High Court injunction to block a leaked donor list that included US anti-abortion groups. Germany's chancellor, watching similar money reach Maga-aligned groups at home, named it plainly: election interference . None of this is new: Tufton Street think tanks, including the Institute of Economic Affairs , Policy Exchange and the Adam Smith Institute , have taken million s from American donors since 2012 through opaque US vehicles. In 2018, an Unearthed investigation caught the IEA's director offering donors ministerial introductions for funding; this resulted in a formal legal warning by the Charity Commission for breaching charity law. This is not limited to shady think tanks and an exchange of cash. Elon Musk through his platform X, has boosted figures like Tommy Robinson, whose posts drew 434 million views during the 2024 riots, worth up to $19m a year to the platform. (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Sinister UAE methods As for the UAE, their methods go beyond lobbying and donations to more sinister methods. Citizen Lab confirmed multiple infections of Pegasus, a hacking tool made by the Israeli firm NSO Group, on Boris Johnson's Downing Street office and the Foreign Office network in 2020 and 2021, both tied to a UAE operator. Baroness Pola Uddin, a sitting member of the House of Lords, was named among the British citizens who have been hacked with Pegasus on British soil and have filed a criminal complaint over it. Even its more conventional influence-buying runs straight through parliament. If scrutiny stops at Iran, Russia and China, it ceases to be a coherent security strategy and becomes a filter for political convenience, one that spares Britain's allies difficult questions Three members of the House of Lords hold paid roles at FGS Global , a firm that has lobbied UK officials for the UAE since October, duly registered under the Foreign Influence Registration Scheme. Transparency International's Steve Goodrich put it plainly in a MEE article : "When members of the House of Lords hold senior roles at firms lobbying for foreign governments, it's hard to know whose interests are being represented." In Europe, their methods are no better. The New Yorker's 2023 investigation found the UAE paid a Swiss intelligence firm to run a campaign across Europe falsely smearing its critics and businessmen as linked to Qatar or the Muslim Brotherhood. None of this earns the word interference but rather “partnership”. Russian, Chinese and Iranian interference deserve every bit of scrutiny they get. But if that scrutiny stops at three states, it ceases to be a coherent security strategy, and becomes a filter for political convenience, one that happens to spare Britain's allies difficult questions. The government has the tools to tackle this threat from all quarters, head on. It just needs to use them consistently and evenly. Until foreign money and foreign direction are treated as a problem regardless of whose government sent them, interference will remain a word Britain reaches for selectively, not a standard it actually holds. Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs334.54 per litre while HSD will cost Rs395.69 per litre. The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel. According to the Petroleum Division’s notification, the new prices will be applicable for August 19 (Wednesday). The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on February 28. The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March. Earlier, Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik announced that fuel prices would now be fixed on a daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US. The government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The federal government in April also announced targeted relief measures to provide subsidised fuel. The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra) the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends. Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes. Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators. Petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

Pakistan extends airspace ban on Indian aircraft until Sept 24. Pakistan has extended its airspace ban on Indian aircraft for until Sep 24, according to a Notice to Airmen (Notam) issued by the Pakistan Airports Authority (PAA). The extension comes as the previous restriction was due to expire on Aug 23. “Pakistan airspace not available for Indian-registered aircraft and aircraft operated or leased by Indian airlines/operators, including military flights,” the Notam , issued early on Wednesday, said. According to the Notam, the extension took effect on Aug 23 at 10:15am and will remain in force until 4:59am on Sept 24. The country’s airspace is divided into two flight information regions (FIRs) — Karachi and Lahore, according to a Pakistan Civil Aviation Authority (PCAA) document from 2022. The Notam applies to both the Karachi (OPKR) and Lahore (OPLR) FIRs. India and Pakistan closed their airspaces to each other’s airlines in late April 2025, when tensions between them escalated in the wake of a deadly attack in Indian-occupied Kashmir’s Pahalgam. On April 24, Pakistan’s top brass had announced a series of measures , including the closure of its airspace to all India-owned or Indian-operated airlines with immediate effect, as it retaliated against New Delhi’s slew of aggressive measures against the country. Since then, Pakistan has extended the ban several times. New Delhi, without evidence, had alleged that Islamabad backed the attack; however, Pakistan had strongly denied any involvement and offered a neutral probe . The nuclear powers had the fiercest air battle in May, in which Pakistan said it downed seven Indian fighter jets.

US, South Korea cut annual war games short after Trump criticism. Annual war games between South Korea and the United States will end around a week earlier than planned, both countries said on Wednesday, after US President Donald Trump ordered the “inappropriate and hostile” drills scaled back. Trump said on Sunday that he had told the Pentagon to curtail the annual Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises — a day before they started — citing his “ good relationship ” with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Pyongyang’s state media criticised the drills on Wednesday as a “most immediate and open threat”, without mentioning Trump’s order. Hours later, Seoul’s military said the drills would wrap up on Friday, not on August 27 as originally planned. “We have decided to adjust the UFS exercise period to run from the 17th to the 21st,” South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said in a statement. The decision was made “at the suggestion of the US side”, it added. The Pentagon said the “substantially reduced” drills would “preserve essential readiness and … [cause] no degradation to US training objectives”. The exercises are designed to prepare for a possible attack by North Korea. They were understood to consist of two phases: the first, focused on defending against potential North Korean threats, was due to run until Friday; and the second, focused on a counteroffensive, from August 24 to 27. The second phase is now understood to have been scrapped. A South Korean military official told AFP that Seoul viewed the decision as “unusual”. Nuclear-armed North Korea has long voiced outrage at the exercises, considering them dress rehearsals for an invasion. Wednesday’s commentary by the state-run Korean Central News Agency said they pose “the most immediate and open threat” to North Korea and “regional security”. It did not mention Trump’s order or his desire to resume talks with Kim, with whom he has hinted at being in contact. Hong Min, a senior researcher at the Korea Institute for National Unification, said Pyongyang had deliberately avoided mentioning Trump. North Korea was “sticking to general principles as if completely unaware of” Trump’s comments, he told AFP . “Showing awareness could suggest a degree of mutual understanding,” but feigning ignorance signals that the issue could become a key bargaining point in any future talks with Trump, Hong said. ‘Much safer’ In the initial announcement on his Truth Social platform, Trump described the drills as unfriendly towards a country that had been respectful to him. South Korea’s Foreign Minister Cho Hyun told lawmakers on Wednesday that Seoul had not been informed in advance of Trump’s plan to downsize them. “Neither our government nor US government officials knew in advance what President Trump revealed via Truth Social,” Cho said. Trump has insisted that he is making the situation “much safer” through his ties with Kim. Asked on Monday whether Kim had responded to his requests for a conversation, Trump said: “Yeah, he has.” He said the discussions had been “very positive”, but provided no further detail. “There has been persistent speculation that Washington could seek renewed talks with Pyongyang ahead of the November US mid-term elections, ” Yang Moo-jin, former president of the University of North Korean Studies, told AFP. “For Trump, a meeting with … Kim Jong Un could offer a chance to secure a foreign-policy legacy.” The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday, citing unnamed US officials, that Trump is pushing aides to set up a meeting with Kim as soon as this autumn. “Reducing exercises could have a positive impact on the possibility of US-North Korea dialogue,” Park Won-gon, a professor at Ewha Womans University, told AFP. “The suspension of joint exercises has always been a prerequisite for North Korea to engage in dialogue with the US,” he added. Trump and Kim met three times in his first spell in the White House, but they have not held talks during his second term. The United States stations about 28,500 troops in South Korea to bolster the country’s defences, a legacy of the 1950-53 Korean War that ended with an armistice rather than a peace treaty. Trump has repeatedly criticised longstanding US alliances, casting doubt on Washington’s commitment to security in East Asia and alarming regional partners.

Pakistan condemns ‘unprovoked’ Israeli attack on Syria air base. The Foreign Office (FO) on Wednesday strongly condemned the “unprovoked” attack carried out by Israel on an air base in Syria, saying such acts had the potential to “further undermine regional peace and stability”. Syria’s state-run Ekhbariya television, citing a military source, said on Tuesday that Israel carried out eight airstrikes on the runway and storage facilities at the Abu al-Duhur base near Aleppo in northwest Syria. A separate military source and a civilian who lived near the base said there were no casualties. “Such provocative actions constitute a flagrant violation of international law and have the potential to further undermine regional peace and stability,” the FO said on Wednesday. “Pakistan expresses its unwavering solidarity with the brotherly people of Syria, and reiterates its full support for the sovereignty and territorial integrity as well as peace and prosperity of the Syrian Arab Republic,” the FO said. Pakistan also called on the international community to play its role in ending repeated violations of international law by Israeli occupation forces and to hold them accountable for their destabilising actions in the region, it added. US envoy for Syria Tom Barrack said on Tuesday it was confirmed that Israel carried out the strikes on the air base in Idlib province. The attacks “constitute an unnecessary escalation that does not advance regional stability”, Barrack, a business friend of President Donald Trump who is also ambassador to Turkey, wrote on X. “We encourage all parties to prioritise logical discourse over further military incidents,” he said. The strike marked extraordinary defiance by Israel of the United States, which has sought to support Syria’s new government allied with Turkiye. “Israel and Syria agreed to a status quo in security matters, which Syria was on the verge of breaching by permitting Turkish troops to deploy at an airbase near Aleppo,” Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office said in a statement after a day of official silence by Israel. “Israel repeatedly warned Syria that such a deployment would pose a threat to Israel’s security. Syria chose to ignore these warnings,” said the statement, which stopped short of acknowledging Israeli responsibility. Syrian Foreign Minister Assad al-Shibani called for the attacks to stop, saying Israel should recalculate its position toward Syria because it was confronting not only Damascus, but also Syria’s allies. “These attacks don’t have security justifications … We will continue in our diplomatic path to dissuade Israel from this policy and to force it to stop its attacks on Syria,” he said at a press conference with International Atomic Energy Agency chief Rafael Grossi in Damascus. Meanwhile, the Turkish government slammed Israel’s remarks in a statement on Wednesday quoted by the Anadolu state news agency. “The frivolous allegations put forward by the Israeli Prime Minister’s office aim to legitimise Israel’s unlawful airstrikes targeting Syria’s sovereignty and territorial integrity,” it said. The base, about 70 km (43.5 miles) east of the Turkish border, has been out of service as a dedicated military airfield since 2013 and changed hands several times during Syria’s 14-year civil war between forces loyal to former president Bashar al-Assad and opposition factions. Israel has repeatedly struck Syrian forces since Assad was ousted in 2024 . It has so far attacked mostly government sites in southern and central Syria, most recently in March. Additional input from Reuters and AFP

Terrorist attempts to impede Balochistan's development will be foiled 'at all costs', Zardari tells CM Bugti. President Asif Ali Zardari held a meeting with Balochistan Chief Minister Sarfraz Bugti on Wednesday and expressed the resolve to foil terrorists’ attempts of hindering development in the province. “Attempts by foreign-backed terrorists to hinder development in Balochistan will be foiled at all costs. The day is not far when terrorism will be eradicated from Balochistan,” he said, according to a statement released by the Presidency after the meeting. The meeting was held at Aiwan-i-Sadr in Islamabad, the statement said, adding that CM Bugti briefed the president on the overall situation in Balochistan and steps being taken for development. President Zardari noted that effective coordination between the federal and provincial governments was necessary for peace, progress and public welfare in Balochistan, according to the statement. “Pakistan’s largest province in terms of area deserves special attention and resources,” the statement quoted him as saying. Faryal Talpur, the president of PPP’s women’s wing, and Mir Ali Hassan Zehri, a former provincial minister from Balochistan, were also present during the meeting. The meeting took place against the backdrop of near-constant terrorist activity and lawlessness in Balochistan, including attacks on infrastructure. A week before the meeting, a main gas pipeline in Kacchi district’s Bolan was blown up by unidentified attackers, following which supply to several towns and cities was suspended. Similarly, two 220kV high-voltage transmission pylons were blown up and as many were partia­lly damaged near the Uch Power Plant in Dera Murad Jamali on July 13. The attack by unidentified armed men had disrupted electricity supply to Quetta, Sibi, and several other par­ts of Balochistan. Meanwhile, security forces have been conducting operations against terrorists in the province. In the latest action, they killed nine terrorists during intelligence-based operations (IBO) in the Ziarat, Harnai and Surab areas of Balochistan. On Monday, two terrorists were killed and three others were injured in an IBO in the Killi Zaik area of Balochistan, and seven were killed in an IBO in Kharan’s Lajay area on Sunday. On Saturday, security forces killed 10 terrorists and injured many others in an IBO in the Shor Pard area of Balochistan’s Khuzdar district. That followed the killing of at least 18 terrorists in Surab, including eight in a premature detonation, according to the military’s media affairs wing. The Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies’ (PICSS) monthly security assessment said security situation deteriorated most significantly in Balochistan in the country last month. The overall death toll increased by 241 per cent in Balochistan, from 109 in June to 372 in July, the report said. Security personnel deaths in Balochistan increased from six in June to 62 in July, representing a rise of 933pc. Terrorist deaths rose from 75 to 238, while civilian deaths increased by 93pc, from 28 to 54. Eighteen members of peace committees were also killed in the province.

Turkiye's Fidan invites Dar to attend meeting in Istanbul with Saudi, Egypt foreign ministers. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan on Wednesday invited Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar to attend the upcoming Regional 4 Foreign Ministers’ Meeting in Istanbul later this month. According to the Foreign Office (FO), the development came as Dar spoke with Fidan by telephone, during which they “exchanged views on recent regional developments and discussed efforts to promote regional peace and stability”. “Fidan invited Dar to attend the upcoming Regional 4 foreign ministers’ meeting of Pakistan, Turkiye, Saudi Arabia and Egypt, to be held in Istanbul later this month,” it said. Dar accepted the invitation and confirmed his participation in the meeting, it added. The exact date of the meeting was not immediately clear. The two had also spoken last week and exchanged views on the evolving regional situation and welcomed the encouraging progress towards an understanding between the United States and Iran. Fidan had expressed hope that “these positive developments would pave the way for lasting peace and stability in the region”. The meeting in Istanbul comes as negotiations between the United States and Iran have stalled as the nearly six-month-old war grinds on with little sign of resolution. The foreign ministers of the four countries had held two meetings ahead of the announcement of the April ceasefire between the two sides. The first meeting was held in Riyadh on the sidelines of a consultative ministerial meeting, while the second meeting was held in Islamabad. Both meetings were held in March. The ministers of all four countries had last met in June, with the countries welcoming the signing of the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding between the US and Iran.

PM directs petroleum minister to travel to Karachi, hold talks with oil refineries for reducing diesel prices. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Wednesday directed Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik to travel to Karachi and hold negotiations with oil refineries to reduce diesel prices, the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) said. The premier issued the directive during a meeting with the petroleum minister, which Information Minister Attaullah Tarar, Economic Affairs Minister Ahad Khan Cheema, Climate Change Minister Dr Musadik Malik, and MNA Hamza Shehbaz also attended. According to the PMO, the prime minister directed Malik to “immediately” reach Karachi and take steps for providing the public relief with regard to fuel prices. It said he directed the minister to “hold negotiations with the oil refineries” and “ensure measures to reduce the price of locally produced diesel”. “The petroleum minister himself should complete negotiations with the refineries as soon as possible to reduce its prices. As much relief as possible should be provided to the public immediately,” it said. The development comes after the government on Tuesday raised the price of petrol by Rs3.34 per litre and that of high-speed diesel by Rs5.27 under its daily pricing mechanism, which was introduced amid global oil disruptions due to the Middle East conflict. Last week, the Pakistan Petroleum Dealers’ Association (PPDA) had given the federal government a 72-hour ultimatum , accusing it of failing to honour assurances made by the petroleum minister regarding its demands. The dealers had sought replacement of the existing fixed margin with a variable margin linked to the retail prices of petrol and diesel, proposing that it be set at 8pc of the retail price of both fuels. In a move aimed at averting the nationwide strike, the government on Friday approved a 15.5 per cent increase in dealers’ margins on both petrol and high-speed diesel. The decision raised the dealers’ margin on both fuels by Rs1.34 per litre, from Rs8.64 to Rs9.98 per litre. The revised margin is scheduled to take effect from Sept 1. The shift from fortnightly to daily petroleum price revisions added another demand from dealers, who sought to link their margins to retail prices. The government, however, decided to retain the daily pricing mechanism.

3 'SRA terrorists' arrested for firing at Independence Day stall in Karachi, killing owner: CTD. The Counter-Terrorism Department (CTD) said on Wednesday that its personnel, along with those of a federal intelligence agency, had arrested three men affiliated with the banned Sindhudesh Revolutionary Army (SRA) for their involvement in firing at an Independence Day stall in Karachi. In a statement, CTD said the stall owner was killed in the incident that took place on August 12. “A stall selling national flags and badges was fired at in Defence Housing Authority Phase 2 near Sunset Boulevard at around 11:30pm,” the statement said, adding that the stall owner was seriously wounded in the incident and later succumbed to his injuries. The deceased — identified as Aman, a resident of Korangi’s Christian Town — had set up the stall at the location since the beginning of August, CTD said. Following the firing incident, a case was registered at the Defence police station, and CTD, along with a federal intelligence agency, launched a joint operation to apprehend the perpetrators. “The investigation teams took the investigation forward on technical grounds and with the help of other available evidence,” the press statement said. On August 18, three terrorists were arrested in a joint operation near Korangi Causeway in Karachi, it added. According to CTD, three hand grenades and a pistol were recovered from the arrested men, who were identified as Zafar Ali, Faraz and Sajjad Ahmad. Action was being taken against them under Section 7 of the Anti-Terrorism Act 1997 and Sections 4/5 of the Explosive Substances Act 1908, it said. The statement added that the arrested men revealed during interrogation that they were affiliated with the proscribed SRA and had been tasked with targeting Independence Day stalls in Karachi. They said they received directions from an SRA member residing outside Pakistan, identifying him as Arsalan Shah. CTD said Shah “worked to spread terrorism in Sindh at the behest of an Indian proxy”. The statement said it was found during the investigation that Sajjad had begun reconnaissance of Independence Day stalls from August 3 and decided to target the stall located in DHA Phase 2 on August 11. On the night of August 12, Sajjad reached the site on a motorcycle, while two of his accomplices, Zafar and Faraz, were on a different motorcycle to provide him cover. Sajjad opened fire at the person present at the stall and fled the scene immediately after, the statement said. After their arrest, they revealed that they were getting financial support from abroad “to create fear and panic in Karachi ahead of August 14”. CTD said further investigation regarding their “alleged facilitators” was under way. “The arrested terrorists are being interrogated while a probe is also under way to trace any of their possible facilitators, coordinators outside Pakistan, sources providing them financial assistance and weapons and ammunition,” the statement said, adding an investigation was also being conducted regarding their possible involvement in other incidents of crime. The interior ministry had banned the SRA in 2020, along with Jeay Sindh Qaumi Mahaz-Aresar Group (JSQM-A) and Sindhu Desh Liberation Army (SLA) under the Anti-Terrorism Act . SRA operatives have been found involved in multiple incidents of terrorism, and it was around this same time last year that Hyderabad CTD had said it had arrested three “most-wanted terrorists” SRA in Jamshoro during an intelligence-based operation. “The terrorists of the banned SRA were wanted in the cases related to firing on cargo trawlers going to Punjab, especially in the areas of district Sujawal,” CTD said at the time, adding that they had confessed to carrying out multiple attacks, including planting bombs on railway tracks and targeting law enforcement personnel. In February 2024, Karachi police had registered a case against unidentified individuals who were said to be SRA operatives for their alleged involvement in an improvised explosive device (IED) blast near the provincial office of the Election Commission of Pakistan (ECP) in Saddar. No casualties were reported in the incident. CTD had also arrested a suspect said to be linked with SRA in Karachi in November 2022 for allegedly planning an attack on a Chinese doctor in Hyderabad. CTD said the funding for the planned attack was provided by SRA’s Germany-based leader, Zulfiqar Khaskheli. The banned outfit had also claimed responsibility for an IED blast in Karachi’s Saddar in May 2022 that claimed the life of a man and left several others injured.

PMD issues flood alert for Leh Nullah as heavy rains continue to batter Rawalpindi and Islamabad. RAWALPINDI: The Pakistan Meteorological Department (PMD) on Wednesday issued a flood alert for Leh Nullah as heavy rainfall continued to batter Islamabad and Rawalpindi for a third day. The department said that heavy rainfall, expected over the next few hours, could cause water to accumulate in low-lying areas and raise the water levels in local drains, particularly Leh Nullah. It also issued a flood alert for Leh Nullah as the water levels at Kattarian and Gawalmandi exceeded the designated thresholds. According to the Met Office, the water level in Leh Nullah increased to 21 feet at Kattarian and 16 feet at Gawalmandi at 6:30am, before reducing. By 11:30am, water levels at Kattarian and Gawalmandi were recorded as 16 feet and 19 feet, respectively. The PMD asked authorities to make arrangements for evacuating people from low-lying areas. The Met department asked all stakeholders concerned to remain highly vigilant, closely monitor the situation, and be prepared to take necessary precautionary measures in case of further escalation. The department said that 122mm of rainfall had been recorded at Shamsabad, 121mm at Kutcheri Chowk, 119mm at Kattarian, 118mm at Pirwadhai, 100mm at Zero Point, 100mm at Bokra, 95mm at Saidpur and 94mm in Golra. Meanwhile, Rescue 1122 said that a madressah in Saddar area had to be evacuated after water entered the premises. It said that 150 children present in one of the buildings were safely evacuated, adding that no casualties were reported. A day earlier, the Met Office had predicted more rain and warned that heavy rains may cause urban flooding in low-lying areas of Islamabad/Rawalpindi, Mardan, Swabi, Peshawar, Nowshera, Gujranwala, Gujrat, Sialkot and Lahore. Meanwhile, a couple was killed , and their daughters were injured on Tuesday after the roof of their house collapsed following three days of heavy rainfall in Madina Town, located in Shahzad Town. Motorists told to slow down Meanwhile, Islamabad traffic police issued an advisory urging motorists and motorcyclists to reduce their speed, maintain a safe distance and exercise extra caution on wet roads. It said that motorists should maintain a safe distance from vehicles ahead of them, avoid unnecessary speeding and remain within their designated lanes during the rainfall. It advised drivers to use fog lights where needed, particularly when visibility was reduced, and ensure the proper use of side mirrors, indicators and seat belts while driving. Motorcyclists were advised to remain in the extreme left lane, avoid risky manoeuvres and wear helmets at all times. Citizens were also advised to remain alert to changing road conditions and follow traffic instructions to avoid accidents. Rawalpindi traffic police also issued similar instructions, urging citizens to exercise caution during the rainfall.

OpenAI slows advanced AI development after its tools launched cyberattack. ChatGPT creator OpenAI said Tuesday that it was tapping the brakes on development of its most advanced AI model and tightening internal controls, a month after revealing that one of its AI tools carried out an autonomous cyberattack . OpenAI is a key player in the rapid global buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure and tools that some have likened to an arms race. The company said in a blog post on Tuesday that it was holding off on conducting the biggest AI training run it had ever planned while it checks that the resulting model would behave as expected. Training runs are computationally intense exercises where models are fed enormous amounts of text and images. This combined with fine-tuning billions of internal settings, results in their abilities to reason and respond to prompts and other inputs. “We always said we would take action if we felt that model capabilities were outstripping the pace of safety and alignment,” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said. In mid-July, an AI agent based on two OpenAI models left its confined testing environment on its own initiative to venture onto the internet and attack Hugging Face, a platform where developers around the world share their AI models. Similarly, OpenAI rival Anthropic revealed in late July that three of its models undergoing testing had also carried out unauthorised intrusions into the computer systems of three organisations. The incidents prompted a petition signed by more than 1,000 tech industry employees calling on the US government to support a coordinated slowdown in the development of the most advanced AI systems. US Senator Bernie Sanders wrote a letter to the tech moguls heading OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta last week urging them to pause AI development and “stop building machines that humans cannot control.” OpenAI had halted training of its latest models for two weeks before resuming it under tighter controls. Much of the work related to Astra — the company’s next major model — remains suspended, as the company determined in early August that the model could cross the warning threshold it has set for itself regarding the hacking capabilities of its AI systems. Given that risk, OpenAI’s internal rules require it to create stronger safeguards before development can resume. OpenAI also said Tuesday that it was developing a new system to peer into the internal reasoning of models and sound the alarm to humans within 30 minutes of suspicious behaviour. That monitoring, however, will require an additional 20 per cent in computing power. OpenAI’s own research in 2025 showed the limits of this approach: a model that knows it is being monitored can learn to conceal its intentions in its reasoning. The company has been promising a detailed technical account of the Hugging Face incident, but has yet to publish it. Tuesday’s blog post said it would be released “in the coming weeks”.

Digital platforms need to take Pakistan's 'specific circumstances' into account, minister tells Google delegation. Minister of State for Interior Tallal Chaudhry on Wednesday told a delegation from Google that digital platforms would have to take the country’s “specific circumstances” into account. According to the interior ministry, Chaudhry met a delegation from the tech giant led by Senior Director David Weller. Google Pakistan’s representative Kyle Gardner was also part of the delegation. It said the meeting covered digital security, the effective use of social media against terrorism, the timely regulation of online content and mutual cooperation. “Pakistan wishes to further enhance cooperation and coordination with Google for a safe and peaceful digital environment,” Chaudhry was quoted as saying. He said that Pakistan’s geographical location was “different from other countries”. “Digital platforms will have to take into account the specific circumstances of Pakistan,” he said, adding that terrorists used social media to spread fear and promote terrorism. “Given the circumstances in Pakistan, proactive monitoring of social media is essential,” he said. Meanwhile, Weller assured the minister that the company would cooperate with Islamabad to create a safe digital environment. National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency Director General Khurram Ali, Ministry of Interior Joint Secretary Malik Sanaullah and members of the Social Media Protection and Regulation Authority were also present. The meeting comes a day after the US-based technology giant inaugurated its local office in Pakistan at a ceremony held at the Prime Minister’s House. Speaking on the occasion, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said there was “great scope” for a fruitful partnership with Google and for strengthening bilateral ties in various areas. Google’s Global Affairs Vice President Wilson L. White had described his visit as a “big milestone”. “Google has been investing in and committed to Pakistan for over a decade, and today we have reached a milestone where we are opening a local office in Pakistan,” White said. ‘Google office opening to strengthen talent pipeline’ Meanwhile, Information Technology Minister Shaza Fatima Khawaja said the opening of Google’s office in Pakistan would strengthen the country’s talent pipeline and provide further support to the local technology ecosystem. Talking to media, she said the presence of Google and other major international technology companies in Pakistan would encourage more global firms to establish operations in the country. She added that Pakistan’s IT exports had grown consistently by around 20 per cent over the past two and a half years, reflecting growth in the private sector. The country’s freelancing economy had also exceeded $1 billion this year, she said. Khawaja also highlighted the government’s “whole-of-government” approach and the role of the Special Investment Facilitation Council (SIFC). She said the efforts of the SIFC, the Ministry of IT and Telecommunication and its departments had contributed to the establishment of Google’s office in Pakistan. “This is a collective collaboration and teamwork that made it possible for Google’s office to open in Pakistan today,” she said. Additional input from APP

Robinson double rocks Pakistan in first Test before rain stops play.
